activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character.
story:
The kitchen table at Nika's house was scattered with index cards, a psychology paperback, and the last third of a pizza that nobody was going to finish. Chloe had come over to work on their health project, but the project had stalled forty minutes ago, and now she was staring at her phone at a text she had typed and deleted four times.

"It's still about Malia," Nika said, not looking up from her cards. Nika was the only one who called their club volleyball setter by her first name, which somehow made everything harder.

"She's going to tank the season if nobody says anything." Chloe turned the phone face down. "She missed practice twice last week and shows up late to warmups, and then in the game she acts like we're the ones being unfair."

"So say that to her."

"I tried. Sort of." Chloe pulled the phone back up and showed Nika the draft. It read: You always mess up the timing and you don't even care, and honestly it's exhausting for everyone.

Amin leaned across the table, read it, and winced. "You're going to make her cry."

"That's the problem. If I soften it, she won't hear it. If I don't, she'll quit." Chloe had a presentiment about the whole thing, a flat certainty that whatever she sent would end in tears, hers or Malia's, and she couldn't tell which.

Amin, who had been quiet since his second slice, tapped the paperback. "That book you brought. Didn't you say it had a chapter on this?"

She had checked it out because Mr. Sok had put it on a list for the project, a book about relationships by a psychologist named Gottman. She'd skimmed the chapter on conflict that morning, half listening, but now she pulled it toward her and found the page again. She read it twice, then a third time, dragging her finger down the paragraph.

"Here," she said. "Psychologist John Gottman distinguishes a complaint, which addresses a specific behavior, from criticism, which attacks the person's character." She looked up. "That's the whole thing. My draft isn't a complaint. It's criticism."

"Meaning what?" Nika set down her cards.

"Meaning 'you always mess up' goes after who she is. 'You missed practice twice' just says what happened." Chloe held the book open between them like evidence. "One of them a person can fix. The other one, all they can do is defend themselves."

Amin pulled the phone toward him and started typing before she could stop him. He deleted the whole draft, which felt violent, and began again. "Okay. So we only say the behavior."

"And one thing about what it costs us," Chloe said, "but not, like, 'you're exhausting.' More like 'when you're late, we run the whole warmup short.'" She watched him type it and realized she was holding her breath.

They worked through three versions. The first was so careful it said almost nothing. The second slipped back into always and never, words that felt true in the moment but that Chloe recognized, on inspection, as specious; they sounded strong and described nothing that had actually happened on any specific day. The third one just stated things. Missed practice twice on Tuesday and Thursday. Warmup cut short. I want us in the finals and I think we need you at full timing for that.

"It's short," Nika said.

"Specific is short," Amin said, and then looked embarrassed, as though he'd claimed more authority than he'd earned.

Chloe took the phone back and read it once more. She had spent two years believing that honesty and kindness pulled in opposite directions, that truth was a knife you could only dull, and now she wasn't sure the two were opposed at all. Maybe they were just different skills, and she had been bad at one and used that as an excuse to skip the other. She would not pretend the thought settled everything. There was still the question of whether she was the right person to send this, whether a co-captain who missed her own serve half the time had standing to say anything. She did not introspect her way out of that one, and she didn't try.

"Do it," Nika said.

"Do what?"

"Send it. Or don't, but stop reading it like it's going to change."

Chloe pressed send, then set the phone in the middle of the table, between the index cards and the cold pizza, where all three of them could watch it. When it buzzed, two minutes later, none of them moved to pick it up.

Amin reached over and turned it face up.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parking facing downhill next to a curb, turning the front wheels toward the curb means the car will roll into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail.
story:
Jake stood in line at the bank on Fairmount Avenue with a folded check from the hardware store in his back pocket. The job started Monday, stocking shelves and running deliveries, and the manager had said twice on the phone that deliveries meant driving the van, which meant a license. Jake had his permit and nine weeks of practice, most of it in the elementary school parking lot after dark, and a road test scheduled for Thursday morning. The line moved slowly. Ahead of him a woman was disputing a wire transfer fee, and the teller kept saying the same sentence in the same tone, like a person reading from a script she no longer believed in. Jake took out his phone.

A message from Carolyn sat at the top of the screen, sent twenty minutes earlier while she was still sitting in the parking lot outside the test center. "Failed," it began. "Everything was fine until the last part. He made me parallel park facing downhill next to a curb on Ridge Street, and then he asked me which way the front wheels should point. I said away from the curb, toward the street, because that seemed like the direction you'd want to go when you pull out. He said, 'Toward the curb, please.' I asked him why and he just marked his sheet and said, 'Wheels toward the curb means the car will roll into the curb, not into traffic, if the brakes fail.' Then he told me to drive back to the lot. I have to retake it in two weeks. How is your practice going?" Jake read the message twice, then a third time, while the line inched forward. He had practiced parallel parking maybe forty times, on flat ground every time, and no one had ever said a word to him about hills.

At the counter he deposited the check, opened the account, and signed his name three times on three different forms. The teller told him his debit card would arrive within a week. On the walk home he called Ms. Nikolaidis, the retired teacher from two doors down who owned the faded blue Civic he had been learning in. She had taught chemistry for thirty-one years and now spent her mornings grading practice tests for a driving school, though she no longer instructed. He asked whether her street had any slope to it.

"Ridge Street," she said. "Steep enough." She agreed to meet him there at six with the car keys, and she added, before he could ask, "I'm not instructing. You drive. I'll sit." That was the arrangement she had set from the beginning, and she had never once broken it, not when he ground the gears of his father's truck, not when he froze at the Route 9 merge with a logging truck filling the mirror. She believed, she'd told him once, that a person who is told what to do at every moment learns only how to be told, which was a way of thinking Jake had rolled around for weeks without deciding whether he believed it too. His father believed the opposite: drill it until it's automatic, subjugate your nerves to the pattern, and the pattern will save you. Two theories, and Jake had been quietly trying to hold both, using his father's repetition on flat streets and Ms. Nikolaidis's silence in traffic.

Ridge Street fell toward the river in one long grade. Jake pulled up alongside an empty stretch of curb, checked his mirrors, reversed, and brought the Civic in close, straightening it out with the small corrections he'd drilled until they felt like nothing. Then he stopped and sat there. The car faced downhill. He turned the wheel away from the curb, the way Carolyn had said, toward the street, because that still felt right to him, the direction of leaving. He looked over at Ms. Nikolaidis. She looked back and raised one hand, palm up, as if waiting for something.

"Carolyn failed for this," he said. "Wheels facing downhill. She said away, the examiner said toward the curb." He turned the wheel the other way, toward the curb, until the fronts were angled in, and then, with the engine idling and his foot on the brake, he thought about what he'd actually chosen. He eased off the brake. The car shifted, rolled a few inches, and the front tire touched the curb and stopped. He put his foot back on the brake and sat looking at the tire against the concrete. If the brakes failed entirely, the car would go where the wheels pointed, and the wheels pointed at the curb, not out into the road where the traffic came up the hill. It was not magic and it was not obvious. It was just a decision someone had made about which failure was the better one to have.

"I guess that's it," he said.

"Put it in park and we'll do the merge," Ms. Nikolaidis said.

He drove down Ridge to the on-ramp and merged onto the highway in a gap between a school bus and a delivery truck, accelerating until the needle passed sixty. The traffic ahead was heavy and his plan, still inchoate, was to hold the lane and pass the bus before the exit. Ms. Nikolaidis watched the mirrors on her side and said nothing. Somewhere behind them the blue Civic's wheels pointed toward a curb on a hill, and Jake thought about Thursday, and Carolyn's two weeks, and the check clearing in his new account, and then the exit came up on the right and he signaled.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A violin's four strings are tuned in perfect fifths to G, D, A and E, from lowest to highest.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and cut grass, and Vanessa sat on an overturned milk crate with a rented violin that was older than her mother. She had wanted the cello, honestly, but the cello cost more per month than her shifts at the bakery could cover, and the violin came free from Mr. Asante, who kept it in this garage among the fishing rods and the boxed Christmas ornaments. He had said, on the first day, that if she was serious she would come three times a week and not apologize for the sound. She had been apologizing ever since anyway.

The problem was the strings. Every time she set her fingers down, her ear told her she was wrong and her hands told her nothing at all. She plucked one, then another, and the notes slid past each other in no order she could hold. Two weeks in, she still could not say which string was which. She had a theory about herself, that she liked to dichotomize things, right or wrong, good or terrible, and the violin refused every version of that. Four strings, and each one wrong in its own particular way.

Mr. Asante did not explain things. That was the arrangement, though she had never signed anything, no affidavit, no form. He sat in the lawn chair by the workbench and listened with his eyes closed, and when she stopped he opened them and waited. "Play the fat one," he said that afternoon. She played it. "Now the skinny one." She found it, the thin E at the far edge. "They're tuned in perfect fifths," he said, and nothing more, as if she were supposed to already know what that meant, or go find out.

She went home and sat on her bed with her phone and the garage still under her fingernails, and she worked it out the way she worked out anything, stubbornly, alone. G, D, A, E, from lowest to highest, each string a perfect fifth above the last. She wrote the letters on her wrist in pen, then washed them off, then wrote them again. She kept drifting, so she built a sentence out of it, something she could say to herself in the dark before her fingers even touched the strings: from the fat one upward, G, D, A, E, each one a perfect fifth above its neighbor. It was not clever. It was only true, and it worked.

By Thursday she could find every string without looking. She told Robert this at lunch, and Timothe leaned across the table and asked what a fifth even was, and she started to answer and then stopped, because she could hear it but not say it, the bright even distance between G and D, like fence posts the same width apart all the way up a hill. "It's the space between the strings," she said finally. "G to D to A to E. The same space, each time." Timothe nodded slowly, the way he nodded at things he half understood, and she liked him for not pretending more.

From the doorway of the garage that evening, before either of them noticed she was there, her mother watched. She had driven over on her way from work, meaning to sit in the car, and had found herself instead at the edge of the light. Vanessa had her bow on the A string and was saying the letters under her breath, G, D, A, E, like a spell, and then drawing a note that wavered and steadied and held. Mr. Asante's eyes were closed. The garage was cold in the way of early spring, a boreal kind of cold that came up through the concrete floor, and Vanessa was wearing the same thin jacket she refused to replace, and none of it seemed to matter to her at all.

Her mother thought about the cello, which she had said no to in October, and about the money, which was the true reason and also not the whole reason. She had wanted Vanessa to want something safer, something with an answer key, and here was her daughter in a cold garage making sounds that were not safe at all, sounds that could go anywhere. Mr. Asante opened his eyes and saw the mother in the doorway and gave her a small nod, which she returned, and neither of them said anything, and Vanessa, still playing, noticed nothing except the string under her fingers.

When she finished, Vanessa turned and nearly dropped the bow. "Mom. How long have you been standing there?"

"Long enough." Her mother came in and put her hand flat on the workbench, steadying herself on something. "It's cold in here."

"I know." Vanessa looked at her violin, then at the door, then back. "Mr. Asante says the cold is good for the strings. I don't actually know if that's true or if he just likes the cold."

Her mother laughed, one short note, surprising them both. She did not say she was sorry about the cello. She did not say anything about money, or about next year, or about the college forms stacked unopened on the kitchen table. Instead she pulled the other lawn chair over from the wall and sat down in it, dusting it off first with the flat of her hand.

"Play the one you were just playing," she said. "The A."

Vanessa set the bow back on the string and drew it across, and the note came out clean.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: The 17th edition of the Chicago Manual of Style, published in 2017, began discouraging 'ibid.' in favor of shortened citations that repeat the author and a short title.
story:
Savannah's grandmother kept the good reference books in the cabinet under the television, below the photo albums and a tin of buttons that had outlived three coats. The cabinet smelled of pencil shavings and the particular vanilla of old paper, and Savannah knelt in front of it on Saturday morning with her laptop balanced on the coffee table behind her, feeling like an archaeologist who had been sent to excavate a term paper.

"What's the paper on?" her grandmother asked, carrying two mugs of tea with the exaggerated care of a woman who had spilled tea on a dictionary once and never forgiven herself.

"The Greenwood district in Tulsa," Savannah said. "The 1921 massacre, and whether the city owes reparation to the families. Like, actual payments. Mr. O'Brien wants an argument, not a report. He said if we write 'this paper will discuss' he will lie down on the floor of the classroom and refuse to grade it."

Her grandmother laughed, set down the mugs, and pulled a dark blue book from the middle shelf. The spine said Chicago Manual of Style, and when she opened it, the copyright page confessed to 1982. "I set type for thirty years," she said. "This book raised me. Footnotes, bibliographies, the whole liturgy." She smoothed a page flat with one hand. "Here. When you cite the same source twice in a row, you write ibid. It's Latin. It means the same place. Saves the reader's eyes."

"It's beautiful," Savannah said, and she meant it, and she copied three of her footnotes into her grandmother's style on the spot, because the book had ribbon markers and tissue-thin corrections pages and it seemed rude not to.

On Monday Mr. O'Brien returned the drafts with a rubber band around each one, which everyone knew was worse than a staple. He had drawn a firm bracket beside each of Savannah's ibids and written, in orange pencil, "Outdated. Check the current edition." In the margin of the last page he had added, "Good argument, though. Footnotes are the plumbing, not the house."

Karina leaned across the aisle, morose in the specific way she got when her own draft came back bleeding orange. "What's wrong with yours? You're the one who reads the handbook for fun."

"My footnotes are apparently from another century." Savannah flattened the draft on her desk. "I used my grandma's book."

"The 1982 one you bragged about?" Karina said. "You cited from a book older than my mom's prom dress."

"Your mom's prom dress is vintage."

"Your footnotes are vintage," Carlie said from behind them, without looking up, which was how Carlie paid compliments.

At lunch the three of them crowded around Karina's phone in the courtyard, out of the wind, and searched the library's subscription page. The current manual, the one the school paid for, was the 17th edition, published in 2017. Carlie, who read faster than anyone and liked to announce findings like a game show host, scrolled with her thumb and narrated. "It says here the 17th edition discourages ibid." She looked up. "So your grandma's book was right, and then it stopped being right."

"In favor of what?" Savannah asked, and took the phone, and read it herself twice, because she had learned the hard way that summaries of summaries were how you ended up with wrong dates in a paper about history. The new way was a shortened citation: the author's last name and a short title, every time, even when the source was the same one twice in a row. No Latin, no cleverness, just repetition.

"It's less elegant," Savannah said, feeling strangely loyal to a word she had used exactly once.

"It's less breakable," Carlie said. "If you insert a footnote later, ibid points at the wrong thing."

"Like telling someone 'same as I told you before' and then remembering you told two people different things," Karina said, and then spent a full minute inventing increasingly disastrous examples until the bell rang.

That evening Savannah went back to her grandmother's house with both books in her bag, the blue one and the laptop, because it had occurred to her on the bus that there was a small problem of manners here. Her grandmother wanted to be the person whose knowledge mattered. She had been setting type since before computers ate the trade, and she asked about the paper every time Savannah visited, and she had gone to the cabinet for Savannah, which in her grandmother's language was a kind of ceremony.

"I have to change the footnotes," Savannah said, and set the two sources side by side on the kitchen table, screen facing her grandmother. "The 2017 edition, the 17th, discourages ibid. It wants a short title instead." She turned the old book toward herself. "But yours isn't wrong. It's just a different edition being right in a different year."

Her grandmother put on her reading glasses, which hung from a chain of paper clips she had bent herself, and read the screen for a long moment. "Thirty years I used ibid," she said. "Ibid was my friend." She tapped the old blue cover once, gently, the way you'd tap an old dog. Then she pushed the laptop an inch toward Savannah. "Change them. Then show me how, because I'm apparently going to live another thirty years and I refuse to be outdated twice."

They fixed the footnotes together, and it took ages, because her grandmother insisted on debating the short titles. "'Report of the Commission' is ugly," she said. "What's the actual title?" And Savannah read it out, and they agreed the short version was still ugly but correct, which her grandmother said described most of the truth she had ever set in type.

The argument part Savannah kept from the first draft, because Mr. O'Brien was right that the footnotes were plumbing. But sitting there, watching her grandmother hunt for a comma with one finger, Savannah found herself softening the paper's ending. She had written that Tulsa owed the families payment, full stop. Now she typed a new final paragraph: that reparation could mean money and could also mean the archive, the excavations, the naming of the dead in official records, and that she could not prove which mattered more, only that both were owed. She sat back. "I still don't know if I'm hedging or if I'm being honest," she said.

"That's the same question," her grandmother said, and refilled the tea.

Savannah read the new sentence out loud once, then printed the bibliography, because her grandmother wanted to pin it to the corkboard beside the crossword, in the spot where the good things went.

"Footnotes and all," her grandmother said, reaching for the pins.

activity: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
knowledge_domain: to calculate the moles of a product formed from a given mass of reactant using molar mass
fact: The law of conservation of mass means the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants in a closed system.
story:
Eli had stayed late for the science fair setup because his own project was finished, and finished things made him restless. The gym smelled of tape and floor wax. Along the folding tables, Crystal was arranging her display board, and at the far end, Cassius was crouched over a kitchen scale with a ziplock bag full of pale powder and a small bottle of vinegar.

"What's the bag for?" Eli asked, because Cassius hated questions and Eli asked them anyway.

"Sealed reaction," Cassius said. "Baking soda, vinegar, the whole thing happens inside. I weigh it before, I weigh it after." He pinched the top of the bag shut and shook it once, sharply, the way you'd wake a snow globe.

Ms. Holloway passed behind them with a roll of butcher paper under her arm. "Judges at four o'clock," she said. "Cassius, is your scale zeroed?" She was not a science teacher; she taught history and had agreed to supervise the fair the way she agreed to everything, with an air of patient amusement, as though the building itself were one long primary source.

Eli had a reason for hovering that he hadn't said out loud. His chemistry test was Friday, and the one problem he could not do was the one the whole unit built toward: given a mass of reactant, calculate the moles of product. He could find molar mass. He could convert grams to moles. But when the problem asked him to go further, to the product side, something in him went blank and intransigent, a door he could see but not open. He had told his father it was fine. It was not fine.

Crystal caught him staring at the scale's display. "Fourteen point two grams," she read. Then she lowered her voice, as if the number were fragile. "You're going to stand there until he does it, aren't you."

"I want to see the weight."

"You want to see it change."

She was right, partly. Somewhere in Eli's head lived the expectation that a reaction that foamed and swelled and filled a bag with gas should weigh more afterward, that all that activity ought to add up to something. It was the same instinct that had made him, in third grade, insist that fire destroyed wood. Ms. Holloway would have liked that as an essay topic: what people believe vanishes and what actually does.

Cassius opened the bottle, poured it in through a corner he had left unsealed, flattened the air out, and closed the zip with a slow, deliberate press of his thumb. The bag bloomed white and stiff, fizzing like static. He set it back on the scale and they all leaned in.

"Fourteen point two," Cassius said.

"It's the same," Crystal said. "Exactly?"

"Law of conservation of mass," Cassius said. "Total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants in a closed system." He said it flat, like a receipt.

Eli stood very still. In his mind the door he couldn't open swung on its own. If nothing was lost, then the grams of product were knowable, all of them, accounted for on the other side of the equation; if the mass went in, the mass came out, and the only work was following it through the arithmetic. Moles of reactant in, moles of product out, each step a matter of molar mass, which he could already do. He felt something loosen in his chest, something that invigorated rather than calmed him, and he had the sudden urge to find his chemistry notebook, right now, in a gym full of folding tables.

"Your face," Crystal said. "You just figured something out."

"Not about your bag," Eli said. "About mine." He explained, half to her and half to himself, hands moving: the test, the problem type, the blank. "I kept thinking the product was, like, extra. Something new that appeared. But it's all just the same stuff rearranged. So the numbers have to balance. I was doing the problem like the bag gains weight."

"And I just proved it doesn't," Cassius said, sounding, for once, almost friendly.

"You proved it for your bag. Baking soda and vinegar. I still have to do it for, I don't know, magnesium burning, whatever they put on the test." Eli was already backing toward the bleachers where he'd left his backpack. He was honest enough with himself to know the gap that remained: knowing that mass was conserved did not mean he could yet trace any given reaction, and Friday was Friday.

Ms. Holloway passed him on his way, the butcher paper finally rolled away somewhere. "Finding the fair stimulating, Mr. Eli?"

"There's a polymath over there with a kitchen scale," Eli said, and she laughed, a short surprised note, and said that Cassius would hate that, and Eli said he knew, and she said, "Carry on, then," as though permission were a real thing you could hand a student, and he carried on, sliding his notebook out and sitting down on the first row of bleachers with the pen already moving.

Crystal came over after a minute and sat one row above him, chin on her knees, watching him work. "If you fail anyway," she said, "can I tell people you learned it from Cassius?"

"Do that either way," Eli said, and wrote 24.31 at the top of the page.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Stage directions in a script are usually set apart in italics or parentheses so actors and directors can tell them from spoken lines.
story:
Gabrielle had never once, in her entire life, been afraid of a blank page. That was the story she told Ayva on the bus to drama camp, and she told it well, hands moving, voice pitched low so the driver couldn't hear over the engine's interminable drone. She was a person who finished things. She had finished a novel at fourteen, terrible but finished, and a portfolio of monologues at sixteen. So the assignment from Mr. Mori, a ten-minute play drawn from a moment in her own life, struck her as a formality. She would write it Monday morning and spend the rest of the week in deck chairs, supervising.

Tuesday afternoon she still had nothing. This was a fact she rearranged in several ways for the benefit of Maeva, who shared her cabin and kept asking, gently, how the writing was going. It was going fine; she was letting it breathe; real writers didn't rush. Maeva nodded each time and slid a clementine across the bunk, which Gabrielle accepted because refusing would have meant admitting something.

The trouble was not ideas. She had a taxonomy of them, pages of them, catalogued by tone: the time her father left, the time she lied about a dog, the time she watched her grandmother's hands shake over a teacup. Every one of them, when she reached for it, felt like a drawer someone had nailed shut. She could describe the moments. She could not stand inside them.

Mr. Mori held his office hours under the willow behind the dining hall, and Gabrielle went there Wednesday mostly to complain about the heat. He let her complain for a while, fanning himself with a roll of script paper, and then he said, "Read me anything. Even the notes." She read the notes. He listened with his eyes closed, which she chose to interpret as admiration until he opened them and said, "The notes are the play. You wrote the truth sideways. Now write it straight." She informed him, walking away, that she would think about it, which was a lie; she intended to write something entirely invented, a shipwreck, possibly ghosts.

She did not get to the shipwreck. On Thursday the camp bussed everyone to the community theatre in town for a first read-through of the older campers' one-acts, real actors from the volunteer company sitting around a long table with coffee. Maeva sat beside her with the programs. The third one-act began, and a thin man with reading glasses read his opening line, and then, in the same flat delivering voice, he read, "She turns away, ashamed." The table went quiet. The playwright, a lanky boy Gabrielle recognized from the senior unit, turned the colour of the theatre's red curtains. The actor peered at his page, then lifted it toward the light. "Ah," he said. "It's not set apart. In a script, stage directions are in italics or in parentheses so the actors can tell them from the lines. This one's just sitting in the middle of a speech like it belongs in somebody's mouth." A woman next to him laughed kindly and found him a pencil.

Gabrielle sat very still. She had been formatting her monologue pages for two years and had never once wondered why the directions looked different, why they sat in their parentheses like small confessions outside the dialogue. They were things that happened. They were things people did when they couldn't say anything. Her whole taxonomy of nailed-shut drawers rearranged itself in her head: the grandmother's shaking hands were not a topic, they were a stage direction. She turns away. He does not look up from his plate. She found her notebook already open in her lap, though she had no memory of opening it.

That night in the cabin she wrote the teacup scene, the true one, her grandmother and her father and the thing nobody said, with the directions set apart in parentheses, the whole fact of it now in her hands. Maeva woke at midnight to the sound of the pencil and asked if she was okay. "I've been fine the whole time," Gabrielle said, which even she could hear was a bridge too far, and Maeva just pulled the blanket up over her own shoulders and said, "Good. Don't eviscerate yourself over it, whatever it is." Gabrielle said she wouldn't, and meant it about the play at least.

Friday she staged the ten minutes with Ayva playing the grandmother and Maeva, volunteered before she could object, playing the father. At the last rehearsal Maeva misread and spoke a direction aloud, "She sets down the cup," and then grinned, delighted with her own mistake, and Ayva laughed so hard she had to lean on the folding table. Gabrielle heard the line land in the empty theatre, the small scripted action in a person's mouth, and understood the thin actor from town better than she had on Thursday: some directions wanted saying, and some wanted doing, and she could not yet tell her grandmother's which.

Mr. Mori watched from the back row with his arms folded. When it ended he didn't say anything for a moment, and she told him she knew it was rough, the middle sagged, the ending didn't resolve. "I know," he said. "Keep it." She stood in the aisle holding her pages while Ayva and Maeva gathered the folding chairs, and Maeva asked, from across the stage, whether there was a copy she could keep.

"You want it?"

"You wrote me into it," Maeva said. "Sort of. Can I have the one where I say the direction out loud?"

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: Java was released by Sun Microsystems in 1995; its lead designer was James Gosling.
story:
The basement smelled like carpet cleaner and old popcorn, and Memphis had dragged two folding chairs up to the card table where his laptop sat open. On the screen was a file called Player.java, forty lines of nothing yet. Jason pulled his own laptop closer and typed his name at the top of a test file, then deleted it, because he did not yet know what he was testing.

"You're making it too hard," Memphis said, spinning a pen between his fingers. "It's a player. It has a name and a score. That's it."

"It has to be private," Jason said. "Fields have to be private, and then you write getters. Mr. Khoury wouldn't even look at it otherwise."

"Private from who? It's our program. Nobody's breaking in."

Jason had asked himself the same thing during third period, sitting in the back of the lab while Mr. Khoury drew boxes on the whiteboard and said the word encapsulation until it stopped meaning anything. The argument on one side was simple: if you leave the fields open, any line of code anywhere can change them, and then when something goes wrong you have no idea where. The argument on the other side was also simple: it was a forty-line program about a game they were building for a class grade, not a bank. He hadn't landed anywhere yet. He typed private String name and felt both ridiculous and somehow correct.

Cassie came down the stairs with a bag of chips and her own laptop under her arm. She had been the one who actually wanted the game finished, since the demo was Thursday and her grade was riding on it as much as theirs. She dropped into the third chair and read over Jason's shoulder. "Where's the constructor?" she said.

"Working on it." He wrote it, then a getter for name, then a getter for score, and then, because the assignment sheet demanded it, a method that added points. After that he instantiated two players in the test file, gave them each a score, and printed the results. It felt like building a small machine out of parts he had only seen in diagrams. When he ran it, the output was wrong, one score twice what it should have been, and he sat with that for a moment before Memphis leaned over.

"You're calling it twice, look." Memphis pointed at a line where Jason had both added ten points and called the add method again inside the print statement. Jason deleted the duplicate and ran it again. Both scores came out clean. He had expected to feel triumphant, and instead he felt quiet, the way he did after solving a math problem where the answer had been sitting in front of him the whole time.

"Who even made this language," Cassie said, chewing a chip, scrolling through the syntax on her phone. "It's so fussy."

"Sun Microsystems," Memphis said. "Released it in 1995. James Gosling was the lead designer. We had it in a quiz at the robotics thing last year. Some kid was shocked it's older than we are."

Jason looked at the year for a second, doing the arithmetic against his own birth year, then back at his screen. Twenty-some years of people writing private in front of things, deciding that this was the responsible way to do it, and handing the convention down until it reached a basement in front of him. He still wasn't fully convinced that the ceremony mattered for a program with three fields. But he had spent ten minutes debugging a mistake that the structure itself had made visible, one number sitting plainly in the output where it didn't belong, and he could see that the fussiness and the findability were the same thing. Maybe. He wasn't sure it would hold up for anything bigger, and he said so.

"That's very epicurean of you," Cassie said, meaning he was making a whole philosophy out of one bug, "but can we move on to the part where it draws the board, because Thursday."

"The board's a quagmire," Memphis said. "We'll sink and die in the board." But he was already opening a new file, and Jason renamed his test class, added one more getter for the player's level, and watched the green bar at the bottom of the screen fill itself from left to right.

activity: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
knowledge_domain: the idea that present decisions can connect to consequences years in the future
fact: Many people prefer $50 now over $100 in a year, yet prefer $100 in six years over $50 in five, a preference reversal called present bias.
story:
The mentorship program met on Tuesdays in the back room of the library, where Ms. Mensah had arranged the mismatched chairs into something like a circle and brought a thermos of coffee nobody else touched. Tyson arrived with fifty dollars in his front pocket, folded twice, from mowing lawns since June. He had a plan for it: a used amp from the pawnshop on Culver Street, one that Mateo swore had been sitting in the window since spring and might still be there on Friday.

Ms. Mensah had other business first. She passed around a folder of scholarship deadlines, and Sami groaned at the essay prompts while Mateo argued that half of them wanted the same story with different fonts. Tyson half listened. When the folder reached him, he saw that one deadline was in October, only six weeks off, and another was in March, and he thought, oddly, that the March one felt easier, more spacious, even though it was the same amount of work. He circled both and slid the folder along.

Then Ms. Mensah, who had been running this program long enough to know when the room was drifting, said she had a proposition. She had a small discretionary fund, she said, for students who finished the year with all their requirements met. She was authorized to offer Tyson fifty dollars now, today, for a commitment to the program, or one hundred dollars a year from now, paid at the next June meeting. Same commitment either way. His choice.

"Now," Tyson said, before she had finished the sentence. The word came out of him fast, the way you answer when someone asks if you want the last slice. Sami laughed, and Ms. Mensah wrote something in her notebook, unbothered, and slid an envelope across the table. Tyson felt the weight of it in his hand, thin as it was, and there was something about the speed of his own answer that sat wrong with him, a small presentiment he couldn't name, like hearing a floorboard creak in an empty house.

He thought about it on the walk home with Mateo. In October he had told Sami he was saving for a proper guitar, and when she asked whether he'd take a cheap one now or wait, he had said, without even pausing, that he'd rather have the good one in six years than the cheap one in five. He remembered saying it. He had even felt a little proud of it, patient, long-term, the kind of person who plans. Six years against five, a year of waiting either way, and he had chosen to wait. Now it was a year of waiting against nothing, and he hadn't even let the question finish landing.

"Read this thing my cousin sent me," Mateo said, pulling out his phone at the corner. He scrolled, then held the screen up. "It's about how people take fifty now over one hundred in a year, but if you move it out far enough, like a hundred in six years against fifty in five, they pick the hundred. Same gap, flipped answer." He tapped the screen. "It's called present bias."

Tyson stared at the phone. The words arranged themselves next to the envelope in his pocket. It wasn't that he hadn't known, exactly; it was that he had held both opinions at once for months without noticing they were the same opinion wearing different coats. The faraway choice felt free, like deciding something for a stranger who happened to share his name. The near choice had weight, had the amp in the window, had Friday in it.

Ms. Mensah answered on the second ring. "I wondered when you'd call," she said, and he could hear her not smiling, which was somehow worse than smiling. He asked whether the offer still stood, and she said the envelope was his, that a deal was a deal, but that she could do this: he kept the fifty, and in the fall, when the October deadline came, if his essay was in, she'd put his name down for the hundred next June. Half now, half later, his patience on a payment plan. "It's not the mathematically best option," she admitted. "It's just the one you might actually do."

He sat on the curb outside the pawnshop, the amp visible through the glass, the envelope still folded in his pocket. Procrastination was endemic to every junior in the district; even Sami, who mocked everyone else's deadlines, had circled two and written neither essay. He didn't trust himself all at once, and that was the honest part, the part he couldn't paper over. But the October deadline was six weeks away, not six years, and six weeks was close enough to feel like now. He pushed through the door, put the envelope unopened on the counter, and asked the man how long he'd hold the amp if Tyson came back Saturday, after he'd written a page or two first.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: The Hindu festival of Holi falls on the full moon of the month Phalguna, usually in March, and begins with a bonfire the night before called Holika Dahan.
story:
Maya's aunt had texted her three times before the car even reached the temple parking lot, and by the time Maya climbed out with her parents, the field behind the lot was already crowded with people gathering wood. Her cousin ran up and shoved a bundle of dried branches into her arms without a word, already sprinting toward the pile. It was the evening before the festival, and the fire had not been lit yet.

"Is that all we're doing tonight?" Maya asked her mother. "Just a fire?"

"The bonfire," her mother said. "Holika Dahan." She said it the way she said everything at the temple, quick and certain, as though the words had been waiting in her mouth all day.

Maya had agreed to come mostly because her mother had asked, and partly because Dale had said he might bike over after his shift ended. She had not been to the bonfire since she was small. She remembered the morning part, throwing color at Isaak until they both looked like they had been dunked in paint, but the night before had gone vague in her memory, a smear of smoke and grown-ups singing. She suspected the whole thing had been desensitized for her by years of classroom dioramas and poster board reports on "world cultures," so that the actual event felt smaller than its reputation.

She found Isaak near the woodpile, stacking logs with a man she didn't recognize. "Do you know why they build it the night before?" she asked him.

Isaak wiped his hands on his jeans. "Something about a full moon. My dad said the timing depends on the moon, that it's not a fixed date on our calendar."

A man standing nearby, one of the uncles who always seemed to be directing something, overheard and turned around. "Phalguna," he said. "The month. The festival falls on the full moon of Phalguna." He pointed at the sky with his chin. "Usually in March. The fire is the night before, and the colors come with the morning."

Maya looked up. The moon was there, pale and already round above the streetlights, and she felt a small jolt of the thing she got in physics class when an equation described something she could see. The festival she had treated as a childhood memory was in fact an astronomical event, pinned to the sky by a rule older than any calendar on her phone. It made her wonder what else she had filed away without checking its provenance, accepting the versions handed to her at school or at the dinner table without asking where they had come from.

Dale arrived while the wood was still being arranged, his bike helmet still on. He stood at the edge of the crowd with his hands in his pockets, and Maya went over to him. She started to explain the fire, then stopped, because she realized she was about to deliver it like a presentation, complete with an opening sentence and probably a concluding one. Instead she just said, "It happens tonight because tomorrow's the full moon. The whole thing runs on that."

"So it's like a lunar calendar thing," Dale said.

"Sort of. I think. I only learned that twenty minutes ago." She surprised herself by saying it that way, admitting the gap instead of papering over it, and Dale nodded like that was the normal way to talk.

When the fire was lit, the crowd moved back all at once, and the heat came across their faces in a wave. The uncles circled the flames singing, and small children were carried forward on shoulders to look, then carried away again. Maya stood between her mother and Dale and felt the two halves of the evening sit side by side without merging: the ceremony with its rules and its moon, and the crowd of neighbors in puffy coats eating samosas from foil trays. Maybe the solemn part and the fairground part had always been the same event, and her old memory of the bonfire as a vague, vestigial ritual was simply a memory of not paying attention.

Her aunt appeared with a plate and put it in Maya's hands. "Tomorrow you come early," she said. "Isaak already promised he'll bring the color he saved from last year."

"Even if it's old?" Maya asked.

"Especially if it's old," her aunt said, and walked off toward the fire, where someone was calling her name.

activity: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
knowledge_domain: voting in an election for the first time at eighteen
fact: The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot because Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856.
story:
Owen had been eighteen for eleven days, which was long enough to feel the age but not long enough to be used to it, and today the county had put his polling place inside the Riverbend Coffee House, between the pastry case and the community bulletin board. He'd been coming here since he was fourteen, back when he was impecunious in the ordinary teenage way and Neveah would slide him the day-old muffins without ringing them up. Now there was a folding table with a clipboard, a cardboard privacy screen, and Ms. O'Brien from the high school, wearing a lanyard that said ELECTION WORKER like it was a rank she'd been promoted to.

"You're on the list," she said, running her finger down the page. "First time?"

"First time," Owen said, and heard how it sounded, like a confession.

Maksim was already at the corner table with his chemistry flashcards spread across two chairs he wasn't using. He worked here weekends and had negotiated his break to coincide with Owen's arrival, which was either loyalty or an excuse not to study. "A monomer," he said, not looking up, "is just the one unit. It's not complicated until it links up with others. Then you get a polymer, and then you get my grade."

"That's inspiring," Owen said.

Maksim turned a card over. "You know what's inspiring? Nobody who has ever voted has changed anything. Statistical noise. You're one datum in a million."

Owen took the ballot from Ms. O'Brien. It was a printed sheet, blue lines, clean squares. He stood there holding it, and the question came out of him before he could decide whether it was stupid. "Why can't anybody watch you mark it? Like, why is that the rule and not just custom?"

Ms. O'Brien looked pleased, the way she did when someone asked about the Federalist Papers instead of whether the essay was really due Friday. "Ask me after," she said. "Not during. There are rules about talking to voters during."

He carried the sheet to the privacy screen behind the espresso machine. Through the gap he could see the window, the street, the whole small town that had opinions about him, and he thought of his mother, who had driven him here and sat in the car with the engine running, and who had said only, "You know what's right," as though right were a single object you could be handed. He thought of his father, who had said nothing at all, which was its own kind of instruction. He thought of Maksim saying one datum in a million, and of Neveah, who had knocked on doors all October for the county candidate and come home once with a bandaged thumb from a screen door. Neveah believed a vote was a brick in a wall. Maksim believed it was a monomer that never polymerized. Neither of them was entirely wrong, which was the problem.

He marked it. He would not describe the mark, then or later, to anyone, including himself, more precisely than that.

When he came out, a man at the counter was telling the cashier he was going to abscond with the little pen on a chain, and the cashier said the chain had defeated better men than him. Ms. O'Brien took Owen's ballot and slid it into the box, and only then, hands folded, did she answer the earlier question. "The secret printed ballot is called the Australian ballot," she said. "Australian colonies, Tasmania and Victoria, introduced it in 1856." She said it plainly, a fact carried like loose change, and turned to the next voter.

Owen stood there with the "I Voted" sticker warming in his palm. Tasmania and Victoria, he thought. Before that, presumably, everyone had watched, or pretended not to watch, and he tried to imagine a polling place where your employer or your landlord could see the square you filled, and understood that the little cardboard screen was not decoration but a wall built in 1856 and shipped, somehow, to a coffee house in Ohio.

"That's it?" Maksim said, gathering his cards. "No thunderclap?"

"There's a sticker," Owen said.

"Give it here, I'll put it on my chemistry binder. Vicarious civic engagement." Maksim held out his hand, grinning, and Owen pressed the sticker into his palm and watched him smooth it down over the periodic table, crooked, right across the row where carbon lived.

Through the window, his mother's car was still idling, wipers on though it wasn't raining. He raised a hand. She raised one back and pulled slowly away from the curb.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: In a 2011 Stanford study, basketball players who aimed for 10 hours in bed nightly improved their free-throw average from 7.9 to 8.8 successful shots out of 10.
story:
The grass at Miller Park undulated in long, slow waves whenever the wind came off the fields, and Thomas sat on the low wall with a spiral notebook open on his knee, watching it. In the notebook he had drawn a grid: seven columns, one for each day, and inside the columns he had written drills. Shooting drills on Monday, conditioning on Tuesday, ball handling on Wednesday, more shooting on Thursday. He filled every square. It looked productive. It looked like the kind of plan a serious player would make, the kind his coach had asked for as a condition of making the regional squad. Thomas was sixteen and had never planned anything longer than a week in his life.

Eshaan dropped onto the wall beside him and leaned over the page. "You've got something written every single day," he said. "Even Sunday."

"Sunday's a light day," Thomas said. "Just an hour of free throws."

"That's not light. That's just smaller." Eshaan took the pen out of Thomas's hand and tapped it against the empty margin. "You know what my cousin did when he trained for the half marathon? He hurt himself in week two because he never warmed up, and then he sat out a month. A whole month, Thomas. Rest days are part of the plan. That's what the plan is for."

Thomas took his pen back. He had thought of training as a kind of arithmetic, effort added to effort, but Eshaan was describing something else, a thing with empty spaces built into it on purpose. He wrote REST in Sunday's square, then felt immediately like he was getting away with something, like a student who leaves an answer blank and calls it strategy.

Zayan arrived with a basketball under his arm and a bottle of sports drink sweating in the heat. He flopped onto the grass and looked up at them. "What are you two arguing about?"

"He's making a training program," Eshaan said.

"Oh, the great planner." Zayan grinned. "Tell him, Thomas. What time did you go to sleep last night?"

Thomas didn't answer right away, which was its own kind of answer. He had been up until almost two, watching film and then, after the film, watching other things, the kind of scrolling that eats hours without leaving anything behind. "That's not part of training," he said.

"That's exactly part of training," Zayan said, sitting up. "My brother goes to that clinic at the university, and one of the trainers there told him about a study. In 2011, Stanford did it. Basketball players who aimed for ten hours in bed every night improved their free throws from 7.9 out of 10 to 8.8 out of 10. Almost a full shot better, just from sleeping."

"Ten hours in bed," Eshaan repeated. "Not even asleep. Just in bed."

"That's what the guy said. Ten hours in bed nightly, and their average went from 7.9 to 8.8." Zayan tossed the ball to Thomas. "And you're over here scheduling suicides for Sunday morning after being awake till two."

Thomas caught the ball and held it against his hip. He looked at his grid, at the filled squares, and understood that he had been planning only half of himself. He had been parochial about it, in a way, treating training as something that happened only on the court, only in the hours he could point to and count. His old coach used to call him a misanthrope whenever he skipped team dinners, but the truth was quieter than that: he didn't dislike people, he disliked the parts of the game he couldn't control, and sleep was one of them. The study said the players only had to aim for the hours. Aim, not achieve. There was something merciful in that.

He flipped to a fresh page. At the top he wrote AIM: IN BED BY 10, and underneath he drew the grid again, this time with warm-ups at the start of each session, ten minutes of dynamic stretches, no exceptions, and two rest days instead of one. "Wednesday and Sunday," he said out loud, mostly to himself. "And a real warm-up, not the two jumping jacks I usually do."

"Look at him," Zayan said. "A reformed man."

"I'm not reformed. I'm revised." Thomas stood and pushed the notebook into Eshaan's hands. "Hold that. Don't read the embarrassing parts."

He walked to the free throw line the park had painted crookedly on its half court, the one with the bent rim that everyone complained about and everyone still used. He bounced the ball three times, the way he always did, and thought about the ten hours, about lying in the dark with nothing accomplished and the body quietly doing whatever it did with all that nothing. He didn't know if he could actually do it. School started at eight, homework ate the evenings, and two in the morning had a way of arriving without permission. But he could aim.

He set his feet, bent his knees, and let the ball go. It hit the back rim, wobbled, and dropped through.

"Seven point nine going up to eight point eight," Zayan called from the wall.

"Shut up and rebound," Thomas said, already reaching for the ball.

activity: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
knowledge_domain: to write a database query that joins two tables to find which customers ordered nothing
fact: An INNER JOIN returns only rows that have a match in both tables, so customers with no orders disappear from its results entirely.
story:
Sophia had told everyone she understood joins completely, which was true on Tuesdays and untrue on every other day of the week. Today was a Thursday. The computer lab smelled of warm dust and the lemon cleaner the janitor used to burnish the desks until they shone like evidence of virtue, and Sophia was staring at a query that returned exactly zero inactive customers.

"That's the answer," said Gregoire, leaning back in his chair with the confidence of a boy who had once argued, successfully, that the sun rose in the west. "Zero. Nobody's inactive. We're all very loyal here."

"Nobody's inactive in a database of four hundred people?" Sophia said. "Gregoire."

"Maybe it's a very loyal sample."

Ms. Villanueva drifted past their row, coffee in hand, and paused long enough to read Sophia's screen. She said nothing, which was her pedagogical method and also, in Sophia's opinion, a kind of cruelty. She moved on. Gurman, two seats down, slid his chair over with a squeak.

"You used INNER JOIN," he said.

"Obviously. It's the join. It's the main one."

Gurman made a face like a man being asked to pick a favorite child. "Try LEFT JOIN and look at the NULLs."

Sophia changed one word and ran it. The results grid filled: eleven customers, names she recognized from the seed data, people with accounts and no orders. Eleven silent people who had existed all along and been invisible to her since first period. She sat with that for a second. It was not a comfortable feeling, discovering that a tool could make absence look like nothing.

"It's not that they didn't exist," she said slowly. "It's that the join only keeps rows that match on both sides. So anyone without an order just drops out entirely. The empty result wasn't the answer. It was the query lying to me by telling the truth about the wrong question."

"That's almost poetic," said Gregoire. "Say it again but sadder."

She ignored him, which took effort, and copied her working query into a comment block. The hermeneutics of it interested her more than she wanted to admit at a desk with a laminated keyboard. In English class you were trained to ask what a text leaves out, who doesn't get to speak. She had assumed databases were the opposite, all numbers, no interpretation. But here was an interpretation hiding in a keyword, a default that quietly erased the unmatched. Two ways of reading, and she had been doing only one of them.

Gurman leaned over her shoulder, close enough that she could hear him breathing through his mouth, which was his somatic signature and how she always knew he was thinking. "You okay? You have the face."

"I have a face."

"You have the face you get when you're about to say something about meaning."

She was, in fact, about to say something about meaning. She said it anyway. "I'm not saying the database is literature. I'm saying I trusted it like it couldn't hide things, and it can, and the hiding is baked in, not a bug."

"It's kind of a bug," Gurman said.

"It's a documented bug, which is the worst kind."

Ms. Villanueva circled back, coffee measurably lower, and read the screen again. This time she made a small sound, approval or amusement, hard to tell. "Eleven customers," she said. "Nice."

"There were eleven the whole time," Sophia said. "My first query just made them vanish."

"That's INNER JOIN for you," Ms. Villanueva said, and wandered off before Sophia could decide whether that counted as teaching.

What stayed unresolved, and Sophia was honest enough with herself to let it stay unresolved, was whether she actually understood it or had merely built a metaphor around a fact. The metaphor felt sturdy. The fact felt sturdier. She ran the query a third time, then a fourth, changing the join type back and forth, watching the eleven appear and disappear like guests at a party she hadn't known she was hosting.

Gregoire was still insisting that zero inactive customers was a defensible thesis. "In some businesses," he said, "that's called optimism."

"In some businesses that's called fraud," said Gurman.

Sophia saved her file. Under the filename she typed a note to herself, the kind nobody would ever grade: the empty result is a sentence too. Then she turned back to the screen, ran the INNER JOIN one last time, and watched the silence where the people should be.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In many parliamentary systems, a government that loses a vote of no confidence in the lower house must resign or call a general election.
story:
The courthouse cafeteria smelled of burnt coffee and floor wax, and Anna had claimed the corner table by the window because from there she could watch the flagpole rope knock against the pole in the wind. Her civics class was here for the morning session of a trial, a contract dispute that Mr. Greco had promised would be "gripping," and so far the most gripping thing was the plaintiff's lawyer saying "as I previously stated" eleven times. Arnaud had counted. He kept the tally in the margin of his notebook, next to a drawing of the judge as a small angry cat.

At the recess Haylee came back from the hallway with her phone held out like a lantern. "Look at this. It's live. The parliament thing." On the screen, a chamber full of legislators was shouting at once, and then the shouting coagulated into a single roar when the Speaker read out numbers. Haylee said, "What just happened?"

"The government lost," Arnaud said, chin on his fist. "It says vote of no confidence. There's a banner."

"Okay, but what does that mean, actually," Haylee said. "Do the police come? Does the army?"

Anna, who had spent two weekends on a comparison essay that Mr. Greco had assigned and then, in a fit of mercy, unassigned, felt something assemble itself in her head. "It means they're done," she said. "In that kind of system, a government that loses a vote of no confidence in the lower house has to resign or call a general election. One or the other. It's not optional."

Haylee frowned at the screen. "So it just ends? Nobody has to impeach anybody?"

"There's nothing to impeach. The prime minister isn't elected separately like a president. The parliament picked the government, and now the parliament has unpicked it." Anna heard her own voice and worried she sounded like the textbook she'd read, so she pointed at the screen where the prime minister was gathering papers. "Watch. He's not going to fight it. He'll either walk out or go ask for an election."

"That's so fast," Haylee said. "Here it takes months. There are hearings."

Mr. Greco settled into the fourth chair with his coffee and a danish he seemed to regret. "I hear the words no confidence," he said. "I also hear Miss Kowalski lecturing, which I would have paid to hear instead of 'as I previously stated.'" He took a bite. "Carry on. I'm furniture."

Anna had liked the presidential system when she started the essay, back before it stopped being an essay. She had liked the fixedness of it, the way a president serves a term whether the legislature likes it or not, the way the two branches stare at each other like neighbors with a disputed fence. It felt sturdy. But watching the chamber on Haylee's phone, watching the prime minister fold his folder closed with what looked almost like relief, she felt her preference tilt. A government that had lost the confidence of the majority was gone by Friday. Here a president could limp on for years, equivocal, half-legitimate, signing executive orders in a basement.

"So which one's better?" Arnaud asked. He had abandoned the cat drawing. "Pick a side. You always pick a side."

"I did pick a side," Anna said. "I picked the other side. I've switched."

"Flip-flopper," Arnaud said, delighted.

"It's not flip-flopping if you have reasons. It's called changing your mind, and it's legal in most jurisdictions." She nodded toward the courtroom doors. "Unlike whatever that lawyer is doing with the truth."

Haylee was still watching the feed. The prime minister had stood, straightened his jacket, and was shaking hands along the front bench, and a caption at the bottom said he would visit the head of state in the morning. "Is that the election or the resigning?" she asked.

"We don't know yet," Anna said, and found she didn't mind not knowing. That was the part her essay had never managed, the part that kept it unassigned: the system itself didn't decide, it only offered the two doors and made someone choose. "It could be either. That's sort of the point. The rule says resign or call an election, and the rest is politics."

"Like carbon," Arnaud said.

"What?"

"Carbon. It's the same stuff but it can be graphite or diamond depending on how it's arranged. We did it in chemistry. An allotrope. Your two governments are the same country either way, just squished different." He looked proud, then suspicious. "That made sense, right?"

"It made unsettling amounts of sense," Anna said, and Haylee laughed into her sleeve.

A bailiff leaned through the doorway and said they were reconvening in five minutes, and Mr. Greco stood, brushing danish flakes from his blazer with the care of a man handling evidence. "Bring the phone, Miss Haylee," he said. "If our lawyer says 'as I previously stated' again, we're watching parliament instead. That's what I call civics."

On the screen the chamber was emptying, row by row, and the Speaker was still standing while everyone else walked out. Haylee pressed play on the volume, and the roar came back, tinny and enormous, filling the cafeteria corner.

activity: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
knowledge_domain: to write and stage a ten-minute play about a moment from their own life
fact: Subtext is the meaning beneath what characters actually say, such as anger or love that a line never names out loud.
story:
The gym smelled of varnish and cold rubber, and Mr. Szabó had pushed the volleyball standards against the wall so the bleachers could be pulled out in a shallow arc. Twelve seniors sat there with notebooks while he explained the assignment: a ten-minute play, staged on the floor with no set except one folding table, drawn from a moment in their own lives. He gave them two weeks. Keira wrote nothing for the first four days.

On the fifth day she brought in a scene about her brother. In it, he came home at one in the morning, seventeen years old, and she was waiting in the kitchen, and they had the fight they'd actually had. He said, "You don't get to tell me what to do, you're not Mom." She said, "I'm the one who covers for you, so actually I kind of am." Both characters said exactly what they felt. She read it aloud on the gym floor with Giovanni holding the script across from her, and it died in the air. Every line landed flat, like a transcript read out at a hearing.

"It's all right," Giovanni said, which from him meant it was not. He wanted the good version, Keira knew that. He'd told her at lunch that if her play worked he was taking the brother role seriously, that he was tired of playing the funny friend in everything, that this was his last year to be seen as something else. He turned a page back and read her brother's line again in his flat reading voice, then looked up. "Nobody in a kitchen says the whole thing."

That night Keira sat at her desk and remembered an afternoon from two years before, before the late nights started. Her brother had burned a pan of onions trying to make the sauce their mother made, and when Keira came into the kitchen he'd said, "Smells like her, doesn't it," and she'd said, "You used too much oil," and they'd eaten the onions out of the pan with forks, standing up, not saying anything about their mother at all, who had been gone six months by then. Neither of them had said they missed her. The scene had been full anyway. She wrote that down and looked at it for a long time.

The next morning she found Giovanni at his locker. "Subtext," she said. "Mr. Szabó said the word Tuesday and I wrote it down but I didn't get it until last night. It's the meaning beneath what characters actually say. Like anger or love that a line never names out loud." She held up her notebook. "My whole kitchen fight names everything out loud. That's why it's dead."

"So take the naming out," Giovanni said.

She did. In the rewrite, the sister doesn't confront the brother at all. She's at the table when he comes in, doing homework, and she slides a plate toward him without looking up, and he eats standing by the counter, and when she finally says, "There's more in the fridge," he says, "I ate at Andrei's," and she says, "You always say that," and he puts the plate in the sink and washes it, which he never does, and the water runs for a while. Neither of them says the word worried. Keira read it and could feel the scene breathing in a way the first one hadn't, though she couldn't have said what was on the page that did it.

Matthias, who was directing his own play about his uncle's restaurant and had appointed himself the class expert, read her draft over her shoulder in the gym and frowned. "It's too quiet," he said. "Nothing happens. My play has a monologue about the health inspector, that's conflict." His play was, in Keira's private opinion, bombastic, all volume, a uncle declaring his life story to a room of customers. Matthias was also, in the matter of food, a genuine epicure, the one person in class who brought cured olives in a tin, and he judged every scene by whether it tasted like something. "Taste this," he said now, handing her an olive, and ate one himself. "It's got salt you don't see. Your scene is just water."

Keira ate the olive and thought about salt you don't see. "That's the point, though," she said. "The salt's there. You taste it after." Matthias looked unconvinced, and she let him be unconvinced, because she wasn't fully sure herself. Maybe she'd cut too much. Maybe an audience would sit there waiting for a fight and get a plate of food and a running tap.

On staging day she put Giovanni by the counter and herself at the folding table and told him to wash the plate slowly, slower than felt natural. Halfway through the silence somebody in the third row of bleachers coughed, and then nobody made any sound at all until the water shut off. Mr. Szabó wrote something on his clipboard. Giovanni dried his hands on his jeans and stood there with his back to her, and Keira looked down at her homework page, and stayed looking at it, letting the moment run a beat longer than the script said, and from somewhere behind her a girl whispered, "God," very quietly, to no one.

activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
knowledge_domain: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
fact: The 'guidance hypothesis' from motor learning research holds that feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helps retention.
story:
The cones were still in the trunk of his mother's car when Ryan realized he had no idea what he was doing. Mr. Zhao, who ran the rec league, had handed him a clipboard, a roster of ten-year-olds, and the sentence "They can't keep the ball, so fix the passing," and that had felt like enough until now. Jameson had agreed to help for the first week, mostly to stand on the sideline and heckle, and Aaliyah had promised to come once she finished her physics lab. The field behind the middle school was mowed into stripes, the grass still wet at six o'clock, and the kids arrived in clumps of two and three, all of them taller than Ryan remembered ten-year-olds being.

He started the way he thought a coach should. Every pass got a verdict. "Inside of the foot." "Look up first." "That one dragged, hit it cleaner." He adjudicated each attempt like a linesman calling offsides, and by the end of the second session the passing drills looked better, sharper, the ball snapping between orange cones in tidy triangles. Jameson, leaning on the fence, said they looked like a different team, and Ryan wrote GOOD SESSION on the clipboard and believed it.

The first game was a Saturday morning, and it fell apart in the first ten minutes. Without Ryan shouting from the sideline, without a correction after every pass, the kids drifted back into sloppy touches and panicked punts, the ball skying off shins and out of bounds. One boy, Daniel, who had been the cleanest of all of them in drills, turned to the sideline before every pass he made, searching, and when he found Ryan too far away to hear, he just kicked it away. They lost four to nothing. Ryan stood at the fence afterward with his hands in his pockets, and the question he could not answer was worse than the score.

He tried to work out the etiology of it that night, lying on his bed with the clipboard on his chest. Not the kids' fault; the passing had been real in practice. Something about the practice itself. He wrote "they only play well when I talk" and then, underneath, "why," and then fell asleep before he found anything. On Sunday he texted Aaliyah, who was the kind of person who read about things, and asked whether she knew anything about why players would be good with constant coaching and bad without it.

She came to the Tuesday session with her phone out and a look that Ryan had learned to be slightly afraid of. "There's a thing called the guidance hypothesis," she said, holding the screen up. "It's from motor learning research. Basically, feedback after every single attempt can make learners dependent on it, so less frequent feedback often helps retention." Ryan read the screen twice. He did not say anything for a while, because the sentence was rearranging the last three weeks in his head: the drills that looked good, the game that didn't, Daniel turning toward the sideline.

He kept the hypothesis to himself, mostly because he wasn't sure he believed it yet, and also because it meant admitting that his good sessions had been the problem. On Thursday he ran the same passing drills but went silent. He stood behind the goal and said nothing for the first fifteen minutes, and it was almost physically painful; the kids were making mistakes he knew how to fix, florid, obvious mistakes, a boy named Theo passing with his toe like he'd never been coached at all. Jameson yelled something from the fence and Ryan waved him down. By the end, though, something small had shifted. Theo's toe-passes had become okay ones without anyone telling him, and when Daniel mis-hit a ball he frowned at his own foot, adjusted, and hit the next one crisply.

The second game was the following Saturday, and Ryan decided to test it fully. He stood at the far end of the touchline, near the corner flag, where none of them could hear a word he said. The first half was rough, honestly rough, two goals down, and a parent behind him kept saying "Where's their coach," which Ryan pretended not to be. But he held his position and his silence, arms crossed, letting the game adjudicate itself. In the second half, Daniel took the ball at midfield, looked up once, quick, and slotted a pass through two defenders to Theo, who finished it. Nobody had told him anything. Theo ran to the corner to celebrate and Daniel stood there for a second, looking at his own feet again, as if checking whether they still belonged to him.

They lost three to two. After the final whistle, Mr. Zhao came down the sideline with his hands in his jacket pockets, and Ryan braced for something, though he didn't know what. "Better," Mr. Zhao said, and then, glancing at the far corner flag where Ryan had spent the game: "You were all the way over there." Ryan nodded and said he was trying something. He did not explain it, partly because he still wasn't sure it was the hypothesis working rather than luck, or kids just having a better day, and that uncertainty sat in him like a stone he hadn't decided whether to carry or set down.

On Monday, Aaliyah found him at lunch and asked how the experiment went. He told her about the goal, about Daniel's pass, and then admitted he'd need three more games, maybe five, before he'd trust it. She said that sounded like the opposite of coaching, waiting to find out, and Ryan said maybe coaching and finding out were the same job. That afternoon he set out the cones early, alone, the grass striped and wet again, and when the kids came trickling onto the field he tucked the clipboard under his arm and walked to the far end, behind the goal, where his voice couldn't reach them.

"Same drill?" Theo called across the grass.

"Same drill," Ryan called back. "You don't need me for this part."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: A pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay; more clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H, and less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B.
story:
Sarah had planned to draw her grandmother's hands for her eightieth birthday, the hands that had shelled peas on that same porch for fifty summers, but the drawing kept ruining itself. Every time she laid her wrist against the paper to shade a knuckle, the graphite lifted and travelled, ghosting grey across the tea cup she had spent an hour getting right. She was working at the kitchen table because the light there was honest, and because her grandmother had promised to stay out of the room until Saturday, which she accomplished by walking past the doorway slowly, sideways, like a crab.

Myah arrived at eleven with a paper bag of day-old pastries from the bakery where she worked weekends, which she arranged on a plate with the seriousness of someone filming a tutorial. "I'm starting a food account," she said. "I thought maybe your grandma's kitchen, the old tins and stuff, it's very aesthetic. Would that aggrandize the birthday thing or ruin it?" Sarah said she didn't know what that word meant, and Myah said it meant make it bigger and more impressive, and Sarah said she wanted it small, actually, which was the whole point, and Myah said fine, fine, but she still took nine photographs of the pastries before eating one.

The smudge problem got worse in the afternoon. Sarah had found a tin of pencils in her grandfather's study, the study nobody had cleared out yet, and she had chosen the darkest one because dark looked serious. The tin was lettered and numbered like a filing system, 4B, 2B, HB, 2H, 6H, in her grandfather's cramped handwriting on a strip of masking tape along the lid. She had taken the 4B and a handful of others and gone back to the hands.

"That's smudging like it's getting paid," Myah said, leaning over. "Which grade did you use?"

Sarah turned the pencil. "It says 4B."
