It said that if an extraordinary event outside the parties' control, such as a natural disaster or war, prevented performance of the agreement, the parties were freed from their obligations. Freed. He sat with that word for a while. The storm had been outside everyone's control, unless you counted the whole town's habit of building in the floodplain, which was a thought he chose not to follow. The school could not give him his lessons while it was underwater. The clause, as far as he could tell, meant it did not have to.

He tried to ruminate on whether this was fair and found he could not sustain it, because it depended on which side of the clause you were standing on. If the school had simply decided to close for a month because the owner wanted a vacation, he would be owed make-up lessons, obviously. But a flood was not a choice. On the other hand, six hundred dollars was not nothing, and the school would reopen eventually, and it was not as though the storm had destroyed his ability to take a lesson on a Tuesday. The obligations, the paragraph seemed to suggest, were excused only while performance was prevented. Or maybe not. The clause did not say what happened afterward. It was like a door that opened onto another door.

He biked back on Thursday. Inside, Ms. Sultani was hauling soggy cardboard boxes to the curb, and she waved him in without ceremony. The office was damp, the chairs stacked, the model traffic light on the counter still blinking its patient cycle of green, yellow, red.

"I brought my contract," Victor said, and immediately felt foolish, holding it out like a summons.

Ms. Sultani dried her hands on her jeans and took it. She read paragraph eleven standing up, one eye almost closed against the light. "You read the whole thing," she said. It was not entirely a question.

"Last night. The force majeure part."

"My husband wrote that clause eight years ago and I don't think a student has ever looked at it." She set the form on the counter and smoothed it flat, and for a moment she looked at the water stain spreading up the wall behind the desk, a brown tide line at hip height. "So. Tell me what you think it means, and then tell me what you want, and we'll see if they're the same thing."

Victor looked at the form, then at the parking lot outside, where the painted lines were reappearing as the water dried, one lane at a time.

"Could I do the last four lessons in September?" he said. "Or I could sweep this office, or both. I'm not asking for the money back."

Ms. Sultani smiled at the tide line, not at him, and pulled a pen out of the drawer. She turned the contract over to its blank back page and wrote, in small neat letters, September, then slid it toward him across the counter. "Sign there," she said. "We'll call it an amendment."

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
fact: Form V cocoa butter crystals melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature, which is why well-tempered chocolate melts in the mouth but not in the hand.
story:
Lily had the thermometer clipped to the side of the double boiler the way a surgeon might keep an instrument close, though she'd never admit the comparison out loud. The chocolate moved beneath it in slow, glistening undulations, dark and deliberate, like something deciding whether to cooperate.

"If you ruin this batch, we're selling lemonade at the market instead," Ryley said from the counter, where she was cutting parchment into squares with more violence than paper required. Aspen sat on the stool by the window, paging through Lily's mother's old pastry book, its spine cracked and softened by years of other people's ambitions.

"The lemonade would outsell us anyway," Aspen said. "Nobody in this town pays eight dollars for a truffle."

"Then nobody in this town has had a real truffle." Lily said it quietly, watching the numbers on the thermometer drift down. The first batch, an hour earlier, had set dull and streaked with grey, soft at room temperature, bending instead of breaking. She'd stood over it feeling the particular sting of a public failure, since the whole point was the market stall, and the whole point of the market stall was the last weekend before Ryley moved to her father's place across the country, a distance so large it had stopped having weather attached to it.

She poured three quarters of the melted chocolate onto the marble slab her mother had left on the counter before the divorce, back when the kitchen still belonged to two people. With the scraper she worked it in long strokes, folding and spreading, and the ribbon of chocolate under the blade went from loose and glossy to thick and stubborn, ductile as wire being drawn. She checked the thermometer. Still a little warm. She swept the cooled chocolate back into the bowl in sections, stirring, and the mass tightened, took on a satin sheen.

"Why the slab thing?" Aspen asked, coming to stand at her elbow. "Why not just melt it and pour it?"

"Because of the crystals." Lily tapped the page Aspen had abandoned. Form V cocoa butter crystals melt at about 33.8 degrees Celsius, just below body temperature. "That's why good chocolate stays solid on the table but melts on your tongue," she said. "Your mouth is warmer than that. Your hand isn't, quite. That's the whole trick."

Aspen frowned at the bowl. "So it's, what, engineered to be exactly body-temperature-ish?"

"Form V," Lily said. "That's the one you want. If you get the others, you get the grey streaks." She dipped the tip of a knife and set the smear on the parchment to wait, and the three of them watched it the way people watch a kettle they don't trust.

Ryley came over and pressed one fingertip to the edge of the first failed batch, still sitting in its pan like a warning. "This one goes soft in my hand," she said. "I've been testing it all morning. For science."

"For eating," Aspen said.

"For both." Ryley's voice had that lightness she'd been using all week, the kind that held something heavier in place underneath. Lily stirred the bowl and thought about how Ryley would be gone by the time the market came around again in autumn, and how strange it was to want a batch of chocolate to set properly this much, as if a clean snap could stand in for everything else she couldn't control.

She waited until the knife smear had gone matte and firm, then lifted it and bent it. It broke with a sound like a small, clean knuckle crack, and the broken edge shone. Ryley whooped. Aspen took the shard and put it on her tongue without ceremony and closed her eyes.

"There it is," Aspen said. "It's gone. It just vanishes."

Lily poured the tempered chocolate into the molds, tilting each one so the liquid ran into the corners, a narrow dark fjord of it sliding down the channel she'd made with the back of a spoon. She scraped the bowl clean, working the last of it out of the seam where the base met the wall, and set the molds on the sill where the light came through. In twenty minutes they would be ready, and tomorrow they would sell them at a folding table under the maple trees, and the week after that Ryley's suitcase would be by the front door of a house Lily had never seen.

"Take some on the plane," Lily said.

Ryley looked at the molds, then at her. "It'll melt."

"No," Lily said, and turned the bowl upside down over the sink, letting the last ribbon of chocolate fall. "Not in your hand. That's the point."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: The Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership, frames feedback by naming when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had.
story:
Mia sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor with a biology textbook open to a chapter she had already read twice, and beside it, on her phone, a half-written message to Manraj that she kept deleting. Last Thursday he had missed the deadline for his section of their group lab report, and she had covered for him, staying up until one in the morning to write his part so Ms. He would not mark the whole group down. She had not said a word about it since, and the silence had begun to feel like a small stone she was carrying in her cheek, something she could not swallow and did not want to spit out.

What she wanted to type was "you're lazy," and what she knew about that phrase was that it was probably true and definitely useless. She had been on the receiving end of labels before; in ninth grade a coach had called her unfocused in front of the whole team, and she had spent a semester believing it rather than changing anything. So she sat there, chewing the end of a pen, trying to figure out whether there was a way to tell someone the truth without handing them a verdict they would wear like a coat.

The handout from Ms. He's class was still in her binder, folded in thirds, from a unit on teamwork that Mia had assumed was filler. She found it now and smoothed it out on the carpet. At the top, in a font that looked borrowed from a business conference, it read "The Situation-Behavior-Impact model, from the Center for Creative Leadership." Below that were three boxes: when it happened, what the person did, and what effect it had. No diagnosis. No character. Just a situation, a behavior, an impact, laid out in that order like the steps of a stoichiometry problem.

Mia read it twice, and something in her loosened slightly. She tried drafting out loud, quietly, the way she did when a sentence refused to behave. "On Thursday, when the lab sections were due, your part wasn't submitted, and I stayed up writing it so the group wouldn't lose marks." It sounded clinical at first, almost like pedantry, and she flinched at how it might land. But then she thought about the alternative, the You always and the You never, the way a general accusation could ionize a whole friendship, charging every neutral thing Manraj said afterward until they were both dodging sparks. Specifics were smaller. Specifics could be picked up and looked at and put down.

Her mother knocked and came in with tea, saw the handout, and asked what it was. "It's a way of giving feedback," Mia said. "You say the situation, the behavior, and the impact. Nothing about who the person is." Her mother made a sound that meant she had her doubts, born of years of hospital shift reports where bluntness was a survival skill, but she set the tea down and left Mia to it.

Mia thought about Walker, who had a talent for honesty with no edges at all. He had once told a girl in their art class that her painting was "not his thing," which was somehow worse than criticism because it gave her nothing to hold. And she thought about herself, about the year she had spent saying nothing to a friend who talked over everyone, and how the resentment had built up in secret, like a debt with interest, until the friendship collapsed all at once over something trivial. Walker's way was too soft and her old way was too expensive. Maybe this was a third way, or maybe it was just structure, a scaffold you trusted until the building was done.

She picked up the phone, then put it down, then picked it up again. Text felt wrong; the words would sit on his screen with no voice in them, no warmth. She pressed call before she could reconsider, and when Manraj answered she could hear a game running in the background, the hedonistic hum of his Saturday afternoon.

"I have to tell you something and I'm going to do it badly, so just let me get through it," she said. "On Thursday, when the lab sections were due, your part didn't come in, and I stayed up until one writing it so the group wouldn't lose marks. I was exhausted on Friday, and I got a seventy on the quiz I hadn't studied for. That's it. That's the whole thing."

There was a pause long enough that she counted it, and the game sounds went quiet, as if he had muted them to hear her better.

"I didn't know about the quiz," Manraj said.

"Nobody knew about the quiz. That's kind of the point."

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: An intersect overlay in GIS keeps only the areas that appear in both input layers, so intersecting housing with a flood zone shows just the homes inside the zone.
story:
The laptop would not stay balanced on the dashboard, so Hailey gave up on it and rode with the map spread across her knees instead, the printed city grid creasing whenever the truck hit a pothole. Three hours to the state fairgrounds, two hours until the submission deadline for the young cartographers showcase, and her overlay was still wrong. Ms. Mwangi had been plain about it before they left: no project entered by noon, no chance at the scholarship money that would make her senior year plans even slightly tenable.

"Pull over at the next gas station," she said. "I need the engine off so I can think."

Corey, who owned the truck and had appointed himself driver by virtue of owning the truck, took the next exit without argument. Ali rode in the back with the cooler and the box of granola bars and, since mile forty, a growing conviction that they had missed a turn somewhere, though she could never say which turn. In the shade of the station canopy, Hailey opened the laptop on the concrete and looked at what she had made.

The map was beautiful, which was the problem. She had loaded the city's housing layer, thousands of small polygons, each one a parcel with a roof on it, and she had loaded the flood zone layer from the county website, a pale blue wash along the river. She had run an overlay, some default tool she'd clicked without reading, and the result was every house in the city, all of them, sitting on top of the flood zone like the water covered everything. She turned the screen toward the others. "So which of these houses actually floods?"

Ali leaned over her shoulder, chewing. "You used the wrong tool, I think. My brother does this for the power company." She tapped the toolbar. "There's one called intersect. That keeps only the areas that appear in both layers at the same time. So if you intersect the houses with the flood zone, you get just the homes inside the zone. Only those."

Hailey ran it. The screen emptied itself of almost everything, and what remained was a scattering of parcels along the river bend, a few hundred maybe, small and specific where before there had been everywhere at once. It felt like turning on a light in a room she'd been feeling along the walls of. "So these are the ones," she said. "These houses, and no others. Everything else just falls away."

Corey had gone quiet in a way that was unlike him. He crouched next to her and zoomed in on the river bend, and she watched him find the streets first with his eyes and then with one finger, tracing east along the water until the finger stopped. "That's my block," he said. Not alarmed, not sad, just stating it, the way you'd state your own height. His house sat inside the pale blue wash, one small polygon among hundreds.

"You said your street never flooded," Ali said.

"It hasn't yet. Not since we moved in." He was still looking at it. Hailey wondered what it was like to find your address inside a shape you'd just learned to draw, whether the information had been waiting there all along, patient, the way water is patient. She also wondered whether the map was telling the truth. Rain had been light for three years; the lawns near the river had begun to desiccate into straw by August; the flood zone was drawn from data older than any of them. A map of risk was not a map of fate. It was a claim, and claims could be argued with.

They had an hour and ten minutes left. Hailey worked fast, labeling the overlay, writing the short caption that the showcase required, and she found herself writing two sentences she had not planned: that the intersect showed exactly which homes stood inside the zone, and that whether the water would ever come was a question the tool could not answer. It was the honest version. It was also, she suspected, the version that would not win, because the judges liked certainty, and certainty was the one thing she did not have. She thought of Corey's father, who had bought that house with money from his own father, a small patrimony passed hand to hand, now sitting inside a blue wash on a seventeen-year-old's laptop screen. Risk had inheritances too, apparently, though nobody signed for those.

They reached the fairgrounds with nineteen minutes to spare, and the parking lot was fuller than expected. Hailey carried the laptop across the grass toward the exhibition hall, and it took her a moment to understand what she was seeing: sandbags stacked along the building's north entrance, a wet-vac being wheeled out the doors, a volunteer in rubber boots pointing people toward a side door. A burst pipe, someone said. The hall floor was under an inch of water.

Corey started laughing before she did, and then she couldn't stop either, standing there holding the laptop with the river houses on it, dry-shoed, on higher ground. "You should enter a picture of this," he said, taking the machine from her arms to save it from the drip line off the awning. "This exact spot, the water and the buildings."

Hailey looked at the flooded hall, at the sandbags, at the map she had a quarter hour to submit, and thought that the overlay of the day's ironies would show only this patch of grass, both layers true at once. "Give it back," she said, already walking toward the side door. "Deadline's in fourteen minutes."

activity: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
knowledge_domain: to explain how DNA is copied and turned into protein through transcription and translation
fact: In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine; in RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine and pairs with adenine.
story:
The after-school lab smelled of agar and the faint lemon of the wipes Ms. Wu used on the counters, and Isabelle had spread her homework across two stations because one was not enough for the mess she made. She was transcribing a stretch of DNA into RNA, the same assignment she had failed twice, and the sentence she kept coming back to was her father's, from the night she dropped orchestra: you quit things when they stop being easy. She had not answered him then. She had a better argument now, which was that she was here on a Thursday afternoon, but it was an argument that only worked if she actually passed.

Abigael arrived twenty minutes late with two cartons of vending machine milk and sat down without apology. "I got a 62," she said. "Emerson got an 88 and he barely studied, which is frankly undemocratic."

"Emerson is a populist," Isabelle said. "He learns whatever the class is anxious about the night before." She pulled Abigael's quiz from her folder, since Ms. Wu had let them review each other's mistakes, and laid it beside her own.

Ms. Wu was at her desk grading, and she had told them on the way in that she would not be helping, that the point of the retake session was to find their own errors. Isabelle had thought this was a bit cruel at the time. She was beginning to think it was the whole reason anyone learned anything.

She read Abigael's transcription line by line, checking it against the DNA sequence. Somewhere in the third line she slowed down. "Here," she said, tapping a letter. "You wrote a T."

"It's a T." Abigael leaned over. "Look, right there, T in the DNA."

"But this column is RNA." Isabelle took out a pencil and, without deciding to, drew two rows: the DNA strand on top, her RNA copy below. "You copy A, G, C the same way, they pair like they pair. A with T, G with C. But when you write RNA, there's no T." She hesitated, because she was assembling it as she spoke and did not want to say it wrong in front of someone. "Uracil. In RNA, uracil takes the place of thymine, and it's uracil that pairs with adenine."

Abigael stared at the rows. "I've done that on every single line."

"Every line," Isabelle confirmed. She went back to her own homework and found, with a small hollow feeling, three Ts sitting in her RNA where Us should have been, which meant the mistakes had been hiding in her work too, all semester, underneath the ones she had already caught. Her error and Abigael's were the same error. She thought of her father again, and of the recording of herself at fifteen playing the Shostakovich, and how she had listened to it last month expecting to be embarrassed and instead had heard a girl who stopped at the hard passage every time. That had not been quitting, exactly. But it had not been staying, either.

Emerson appeared in the doorway with his jacket still on, drawn by some atavistic instinct for finding the room where his friends were, and he dropped into the stool beside Abigael and peered at the two rows of letters. "Is this the thing with the U?" he said. "I lost a whole point to that."

"Whole class lost points to that," Abigael said. She had begun correcting her lines, striking through each stray T with a violence that suggested the letters had personally wronged her.

"Read me a base," Isabelle said to Emerson, and covered her answer with her hand. "DNA. Random letter."

"G."

She wrote C below it, then made herself say the pairing out loud as she went, because saying it was what kept it from sliding back into fog: G and C, A and T in the DNA, and then in the RNA, when he called the next A, she wrote U and said, "Uracil," and heard Abigael repeat it under her breath like a charm.

Ms. Wu drifted over at last and looked at the board where Isabelle had chalked her two rows, adenines over uracils, guanines over cytosines, the whole small grammar of it. She did not say it was right. She said, "Clean the counters when you finish," and went back to her grading, and Isabelle, after a moment, picked up the rag.

activity: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
knowledge_domain: to interview for a part-time job with confident eye contact and clear answers
fact: In a 1999 study, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements.
story:
Gabriel's uncle had appointed himself chairman of the dinner table, which was generous of him, since nobody had voted. Between passes of the rice, he fired questions across the lamb: where do you see yourself in five years, why do you want this job, what is your greatest weakness. Gabriel answered to his plate.

"Eyes up," his mother said. "You're telling the potatoes about your weaknesses, not the manager."

"I'm telling the potatoes I'm a quick learner." He looked up anyway, at his uncle, who nodded like a man collecting evidence.

The interview at the garden centre was Thursday. He had wanted the job since March, when he'd watched a boy his own age carry a rosebush to the register with an air of total insouciance, as if being paid to stand among plants all summer were the most natural thing in the world. Gabriel wanted that. He also wanted four hundred pounds, but he had decided the rosebush version sounded better in interviews.

The trouble was everything else. In practice sessions his answers came out in a mumble, or not at all. Last week Byron had sat across from him in the library and played the manager, and Gabriel had prevaricated so long on the weakness question that Byron finally said, "Your weakness is answering questions," and packed up his bag.

That was before the study. Gabriel had found it in a magazine in the dentist's waiting room, and had read the page twice because the hygienist was running late. In 1999, two researchers, Tanya Chartrand and John Bargh, found that people liked a partner more when the partner subtly mimicked their posture and movements. He'd copied nothing down, but the sentence had stuck to him the way certain sentences do, arriving with its own adhesive. He told Jaiveer about it on the walk home, testing whether he'd remembered it right.

"Chartrand and Bargh," Jaiveer said. "Ninety-nine. Yeah, that sounds like the one. People liked the partner more when the partner matched their posture. Subtly, though. It said subtly."

"So if the manager leans forward, I lean forward."

"If you want to be liked. Which, in an interview, yes."

Gabriel had originally believed that the whole business was beneath him, that rehearsing eye contact was a kind of theatre for people with nothing to say. He'd argued this position to Byron on more than one occasion, and Byron had let him. But somewhere between the dentist and the dinner table he'd changed his mind, or at least softened it. Everyone performed a little. His uncle performed authority over the lamb. His mother performed patience with the uncle. Perhaps the difference between a fraud and a prepared person was only the part you'd practised.

Not that the study settled anything. He was honest enough, at the table, pushing peas into a line, to admit that much to himself. Whether matching a stranger's posture was charm or manipulation, he couldn't decide, and the magazine hadn't either. It had simply reported what happened.

"Tell me about a time you resolved a conflict," his uncle said, reloading.

"Last Tuesday," Gabriel said, "my friend Byron accused me of being a revisionist historian about why we lost the five-a-side final, and I conceded that I had, in fact, passed the ball badly, and we agreed the matter was closed." He held his uncle's gaze through the whole answer. His uncle blinked first.

"There," his mother said. "That's the one about your weakness. Use that one Thursday."

"My weakness is honesty," Gabriel said.

"Don't prevaricate," his uncle said gravely, "and don't be clever."

"Those are the same instruction."

Thursday came in warm and bright, and the garden centre smelled of wet soil and the faint sweetness of cut grass. The manager was younger than Gabriel expected, and she had a way of tilting her head when she listened, so that her pen hovered above the clipboard like a small bird. Gabriel answered the questions about availability without stumbling, and when she asked why he wanted the job, he said something about liking the work being outdoors and real, which was true, and which he had also practised.

Then she leaned forward, elbows on the table, and Gabriel sat still for a moment, weighing it. Chartrand and Bargh, 1999. Subtly, though.

He leaned forward, slowly, as if settling into the conversation, and asked her whether the summer staff learned to graft anything or just watered. She sat back, surprised into a real answer, and somewhere behind her clipboard she started to smile.

"So when can you start?" she said.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Food Banks Canada's HungerCount 2025 recorded nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month.
story:
The notice had said the food bank would set up in the common room of the seniors' residence on a Tuesday, so Vanessa arrived expecting folding tables and a slow trickle of grey-haired residents. What she found instead was a line that ran from the double doors, past the fish tank, and down the corridor toward the physiotherapy wing, where she lost sight of it. Ammar was already stacking crates behind a table, and he waved her over with the relief of someone who had been alone among strangers.

"I thought it would be, like, twelve people," she said. "It's a weekday. Aren't they at bingo?"

"Apparently not." Ammar peeled an orange in one unbroken spiral, a talent he performed whenever he was nervous. "Ms. Hussain said to expect a lot. She wasn't joking."

Ms. Hussain, who ran the pop-up, handed Vanessa a clipboard and a roll of stickers. Residents who had pre-registered got a dot on the hand; everyone else filled out a form. It sounded simple. It was not simple, because half the residents could not find their glasses and the other half wanted to argue about whether they needed to register at all, having come only, they insisted, to help.

Conor showed up twenty minutes late, still in his mock trial blazer, carrying a box of oatmeal he had clearly taken from his own kitchen. "Donation," he announced, setting it down with ceremony. "I rest my case."

"You don't have a case," Ammar said.

"I had an acquittal this afternoon. Full marks for the defence. My client, a man who allegedly stole a bicycle, walks free because I established reasonable doubt about the handlebars." He looked out at the line and his grin faded a little. "Though I'm starting to feel like I chose the wrong side of that unit."

Vanessa laughed, but the laugh felt unstable in her chest, the way a table wobbles when one leg is shorter. She handed out stickers. She learned names: the man with the walker who wanted rice, not pasta, because of his teeth; the woman from the third floor who took only what she could carry in one canvas bag, though her arms shook.

In her civics class they had studied a report called HungerCount, the annual survey Food Banks Canada published, and the teacher had made them memorize a figure for a quiz: nearly 2.2 million food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, a record for a single month. Vanessa had written it on a flashcard, matched it to the right bubble on the sheet, and forgotten it by lunch. Standing here, she remembered it with a strange, physical clarity, the number suddenly occupying space, stretching down a hallway in a building where everyone was supposed to be taken care of. She said it out loud to Ammar while they restocked the tinned peas.

"Two point two million visits," he repeated. "In one month. In Canada." He let the orange spiral fall into the compost bin. "That's the whole population of Toronto-ish, lining up for food."

"Basically," Vanessa said, though she was never sure about her own comparisons, and she filed the doubt away the way she filed most things, next to everything else she hadn't resolved.

Last summer, her mother had driven her past this building twice a week on the way to the pool, and every time her mother had pointed at it without slowing down and said, your grandmother lives there now, as if reporting weather. Vanessa had looked at the geraniums, the tended path, the automatic doors, and had never once asked to stop. It had seemed easier to keep the woman at the distance of a fact on a flashcard. That was before the line, before the shaking arms, before the number had grown legs.

Because near the end of the afternoon, the line having shortened to a dozen people, Vanessa looked up from her clipboard and saw her grandmother three places from the front, wearing a cardigan Vanessa recognized from a photograph on her mother's dresser, the teal one with the missing button. Ms. Hussain was already reaching for the next registration form. Vanessa's hand, holding the sticker sheet, stopped in the air. Her grandmother had not seen her yet; she was studying the display of peanut butter with the penurious attention of someone counting portions against days. Vanessa could have stepped back, let Ammar take the sticker, let the moment pass as smoothly as the car had always passed the building. She thought about it. She was honest enough with herself to admit she thought about it.

Then the line moved, and her grandmother was in front of her, and Vanessa held out the form and said, in a voice she had to steady first, "Can I get your name?"

Her grandmother looked up. For a second there was nothing in her face, and Vanessa braced for the acquittal of being unrecognized, released without consequence. Then the old woman's eyes widened, and she said, "You have your mother's chin," and put her free hand, light as a sticker, on Vanessa's wrist.

Vanessa wrote the name on the form. She pressed the dot onto the back of her grandmother's hand, smoothing it down with her thumb so it would stay.

"Come back next Tuesday?" her grandmother asked, already reaching for the rice.

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: Research by linguist Paul Nation and colleagues suggests readers need to know about 98 percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help.
story:
The article was four paragraphs long, in Spanish, about a drought in Chile, and Brooke had agreed to read it aloud and summarise it at the restaurant where her mother worked, because Saturday was the assessment and the house was too loud on Friday nights. She spread the pages across the counter between the register and the coffee machine, where Ms. Otieno, who came in every Friday for the bean soup, could watch her and listen.

"You promised ten minutes," Ms. Otieno said. She sat on her usual stool and turned her cup so the handle faced the window.

Brooke began. The first paragraph went tolerably. The second paragraph contained the word "escasez," and she stopped on it, then guessed, then stopped again, and the sentence collapsed around the guess. She tried the third paragraph anyway, and it was worse: whole lines where she knew perhaps one word in five, and she could hear herself slowing down, the way a person walks through deep snow.

Landon slid into the booth behind Ms. Otieno with a basket of fries he had not paid for yet. "You look like the article insulted you personally."

"It's not insulting me. It's just sitting there being impossible." She flattened the page with her palm. "I keep thinking if I just push through it, the meaning will collect at the bottom, like sediment. It doesn't. Every paragraph is a puzzle with half the pieces missing, and I don't even know which pieces are missing."

Graeme arrived from the kitchen with his apron still on, since he had swapped shifts to practice with her before Saturday, and read over her shoulder. "This is too hard for you," he said, not unkindly. "Mine's about a football match and I only had to look up four words."

Brooke looked at the article again. Four paragraphs. She counted the words she genuinely did not know in the first paragraph alone: eleven. "How many is too many?" she said. "There has to be a line somewhere. One unknown word and you're fine, and then somewhere after that you're drowning."

Ms. Otieno stirred her soup. "There's a number," she said. "I read it years ago, when I was learning English. Some linguist, Nation, I think, with colleagues. He said readers need to know about ninety-eight percent of the words in a text to understand it comfortably without help."

"Ninety-eight," Brooke repeated. She did the arithmetic on the back of a napkin, fast, the way she did arithmetic, lips moving. If a paragraph was a hundred words, that meant two unknown words. Two, and the paragraph still felt smooth. Three or more, and you were translating instead of reading, which was a different activity entirely, slower and colder. "My first paragraph has eleven."

"Then it isn't a you problem," Graeme said. "It's an article problem."

She sat with that for a moment. Part of her wanted to keep grinding at the drought piece, because it was serious, important, about something real, and the football article Graeme had chosen felt trivial by comparison, a toy. But she could also see the other view: the point of Saturday was not to demonstrate virtue, it was to read in Spanish and summarise it aloud, and a text she could actually read would let her do that, and doing it would build something the drought article, wrestled word by word, would not. Choosing the easier text was not the same as choosing the weaker task. She was not certain of that. She held it anyway, provisionally, the way you hold a belief you intend to test.

"Give me your football article," she said to Graeme.

"It's about a match. You'll be bored."

"I'll be comprehensible." He fetched it from his backpack, and she read it through once silently, marking three words, then aloud. The sentences ran. Where she stumbled, she stumbled once and recovered, and when she finished, she closed the paper and gave the summary in Spanish: the teams, the score, a disputed penalty, the coach's furious comments afterward, which one commentator had called malevolent, a word she'd had to verify and which seemed, to her, too strong for a man merely complaining about a referee, though she supposed dysphemism was the whole trade of sports commentary.

"Not bad," Ms. Otieno said. "You expatiated a little on the penalty."

"I did," Brooke admitted. "It was the part I understood best." She pushed the football article aside and pulled the drought piece back in front of her, folded it in half. "I'm not giving up on this one. I'm just not doing it tonight. Or Saturday. Saturday I'll take something I can read, and after that I'll work up to Chile." She looked at the clock above the pass. Nine minutes gone. "One more time, from the top. Time me."

Ms. Otieno set down her spoon and raised her phone. "Ready," she said.

activity: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
knowledge_domain: to read an ocean current map and explain how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe
fact: Benjamin Franklin had a chart of the Gulf Stream printed in London in 1769, using knowledge from his cousin Timothy Folger, a Nantucket whaling captain.
story:
The planetarium had run out of space topics, so it was showing oceans. That was how Ms. Yoon put it on the first morning of the summer workshop, holding up a folder like it was something she'd found behind a vending machine. "The new projector can map anything with coordinates," she said. "Mars, magma, the Gulf Stream. Guess which one has funding." Justin had signed up because the brochure said astronomy and he had wanted the dome, the dark, the feeling of being somewhere else. Instead he got a rotating blue ellipsoid with white arrows crawling across it like ants on a dropped ice cream cone.

"See," said Zaynab, leaning over his shoulder on the second day, "your problem is that you want the map to be a picture. It's not a picture. It's an argument."

"It's water," Justin said. "Moving."

"Everything on a map is an argument. Somebody decided what mattered." She tapped the screen where the current swung away from the American coast and pointed itself across the Atlantic like a delivery truck ignoring all the exits. "Also you've traced the same arrow three times and it's the wrong one."

Thalie, from the next seat, held up her phone. "I've been reading. Ships crossing to England used to fight that thing for weeks without knowing it was there. Then somebody drew it. Guess who." She paused in a way that suggested a game show.

"A fish?" said Justin.

"Benjamin Franklin."

"Franklin drew a fish?"

"He printed a chart of the Gulf Stream in London in 1769," Thalie said. "Using his cousin. Timothy Folger. A Nantucket whaling captain."

Justin looked at her, then at the dome, where the current glowed in simulated amber above them like a river laid across the sky. "Wait. The postal service guy. The kite guy. He did oceanography?"

"He was postmaster," Ms. Yoon said from the front, not looking up from her laptop, "and he noticed the mail packets took forever while merchant ships beat them home. But don't ask me. Ask your sources." Ms. Yoon had a rule about this, which was that she would confirm nothing she had not personally witnessed, which by her own admission included most of the eighteenth century.

The assignment, due Friday, was to stand under the dome and explain to the group how the Gulf Stream warms northern Europe. Justin had the pieces. He had the map Zaynab kept correcting. He had a paragraph from the workshop reader that began, in prose he could only call turgid, "The redistribution of thermal energy constitutes," and then slid downhill from there. He had Thalie's anecdote, which was the only part anybody would actually remember. What he did not have was a way to hold them together, the argument and the water, the lines on the chart and the actual warm mass sliding northeast toward islands that had no business being as mild as they were.

He tried writing it out Thursday night and the draft kept splitting in two. One half was numbers and arrows, clean and confident, and the other half was Franklin standing on a dock asking his cousin why the London ships were so slow, and Folger, who had spent his life on that water, saying, in effect, because you're rowing against a river in the sea. Justin had always liked the second story better, which annoyed him, because the first one was the one that was true in the way that survived checking. Or no. Both were true. That was the problem.

"You're externalizing," Zaynab told him the next morning in the planetarium lobby, where he had been explaining his crisis to the vending machine.

"I'm what?"

"Putting it all outside yourself so you don't have to decide anything. You keep saying 'on one hand, on the other hand.' You have no hands left, Justin. Pick a hand."

"It's not that simple. It's like, is knowing the current a fact or is it a story about people finding the fact? You can't just, " he gestured at the ceiling, the dome, the general concept of knowledge, "pick."

Zaynab considered this with the seriousness she gave everything, including the vending machine. "My dad says that's what happens when you confuse rationalism with being right. Rationalism is a method. Being right is luck. Folger didn't derive the current from first principles. He sailed on it for twenty years and then told his cousin. Then Franklin put it on paper and suddenly it was knowledge."

"And the paper is London, 1769," Thalie said, arriving with the folder, "in case you forgot the one date you're allowed to say."

When his turn came, the dome went dark and the amber river rose over them. Justin talked for four minutes. He traced the current with the pointer, its long arc off the coast, its crossing, its arrival off northwestern Europe, and he said that captains had been saving days by steering around it long before there were satellites, because a Nantucket whaling captain named Timothy Folger knew the water the way a mailman knows a bad dog on a certain street, and his cousin Benjamin Franklin had a chart of it printed in London in 1769. He said the warm water goes where the arrows go, and northern Europe is warmer than it should be for its latitude because of what arrives. Then he said, into the dark, "Here's what I still can't tell you: whether the map is the discovery or whether Folger discovered it years before, on deck, and the chart was just the receipt." Ms. Yoon's projector light caught her raising one eyebrow, which from her was applause.

Afterward Thalie bumped his shoulder on the way out. "Receipt," she said. "You made a current sound like a grocery store."

"He made it sound like it was found by people," Zaynab said, "which it was. Caps and all." Outside, the summer air sat heavy and warm over the parking lot, and Justin stood in it a second longer than the others, thinking that somewhere under all that heat the water was already moving, arrows or no arrows, heading northeast with or without a chart.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A 'best before' date marks when a food's quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe, so sealed food past that date may still be safe to eat.
story:
The food bank shared a parking lot with the neighborhood cleanup, so Sarah arrived with paint on her sleeves and the smell of mulch in her hair, having already spent the morning dragging tires out of the creek behind the hardware store. Tamara had commandeer ed the best wheelbarrow for their crew and refused to give it back, which was how Sarah ended up carrying bags of trash by hand until Mr. Hughes, the retired teacher who seemed to organize everything on this street, pointed her toward the folding table outside the food bank's side door.

"We're sorting donations today," he said. "You'll be great at it. It's basically the creek, but with cans."

Inside, a woman with a clipboard handed Sarah a box and a bin. Donations in the box, trash in the bin, and anything questionable set aside for her to look at. Anaya was already there, three crates deep, wearing gloves meant for someone twice her size and flapping her hands like a surgeon who had lost a bet.

"Sarah, look what I found." Anaya held up a can of pears. "A can of pears. Like, from the previous administration."

The label read a best before date from last month. Anaya tossed it toward the bin, and Sarah caught it out of the air, mostly because her reflexes were better than her opinions.

"Wait," she said. "Are we sure? They just got these."

"They're expired."

"They're..." Sarah turned the can over. She had eaten yogurt two days past its date at Tamara's house once and survived, but that felt like anecdote, not evidence. Anaya was already binning a jar of tomato sauce with the serene confidence of someone who had never once questioned a label. Sarah set the pears on the table between them like a hostage negotiation.

"Okay, but expired how?" she said. "Like poison how, or like, not as peary how?"

Anaya squinted at her. "Those are different?"

Sarah pulled out her phone, aware that this was the least cool thing she had done all day, including the mulch. She typed best before date safe or not and read while Anaya narrated over her shoulder in a dramatic courtroom voice, "The prosecution submits Exhibit A, one can of sketchy pears."

The first result was a food safety page, plain and unimpressed. She read it twice.

"Okay, so, a best before date is about quality, not safety," Sarah said. "It marks when a food's quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe. Sealed food past that date may still still be safe to eat."

Anaya crossed her arms. "So the pears might just be, what, slightly mediocre pears."

"Peak mediocre pears. Legally permitted mediocrity."

"Sold." Anaya retrieved a can of chickpeas from the bin, held it up like a trophy, and then, with the gravity of a judge issuing a subpoena, intoned, "Chickpea v. Trash Bin. The court finds the defendant sealed and delicious. Case dismissed."

They worked backward through the bin for ten minutes, rescuing cans a week or two past their dates, until the woman with the clipboard came over and cleared her throat.

"Sorry," Sarah said. "We're putting expired stuff back. Is that wrong? We looked it up, best before is quality, not safety, so if it's sealed it might still be fine, but if you have to throw it out anyway, we totally understand, we'll..."

The woman was laughing. "Sweetheart, we know. We keep all of that. There's a separate shelf. I keep telling the weekend volunteers and they keep binning everything anyway. Last month someone threw out forty cans of soup."

"Forty," Anaya whispered, hand on her chest. "There were survivors' families."

The twist, when it came, arrived in a cardboard box. Mr. Hughes stuck his head in the door near the end of the shift and said the cleanup crew had found a sealed case of canned vegetables behind the fence at the old lot, sun-bleached labels, dates from months back, and did the food bank want it or should he leave it by the curb. The clipboard woman looked at Sarah and Anaya and raised one eyebrow, an affective challenge, an invitation, an entire exam question compressed into a single facial muscle.

Sarah looked at the case. Sun-bleached meant it had been outside, and outside was a different problem than a shelf, one the webpage had not covered. Sealed was sealed, but sealed in what, for how long, at what temperature? She could apply the rule and she still could not apply it all the way down.

"Can we open one first?" she asked. "Like, one can, and if it looks and smells normal, the rest can go on the quality shelf. If it looks like a science project, curb."

"Look at you," Anaya said. "Doubting your own precedent. Very affective of you."

"That's not what that word means and we both know it."

Mr. Hughes carried the case inside and set it on the table with a small bow. Sarah took the can opener from the drawer, pierced the lid, and lifted it, bending close.
